views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Use the G20 90-day window to negotiate structural issues (IP, forced tech transfer, non-tariff barriers) without new tariff hikes and without rolling back Lists 1–3. Keep the March 1, 2019 List-3 hike to 25% as the backstop, press Beijing to convert the vague “very substantial” purchase pledge into dated ag/energy orders that relieve the farm belt, and keep the Meng extradition on a law-enforcement track rather than trading it for a soft deal. Do not reopen a May-style “trade war on hold” pause that collapses when talks get hard.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is modestly positive, not high and not an opportunity. The U.S. still holds the stronger hand—Section 301 now covers ~$250B of Chinese imports while China has retaliated on ~$110B, and the Dec 1 G20 dinner suspended the Jan 1 List-3 hike without removing existing tariffs—but costs are no longer theoretical. China’s 25% soybean tariff has cut U.S. shipments sharply (September imports from the U.S. down >80%; mid-October sales down ~94% y/y; USDA forecasting ag exports to China down $7B in FY2019), and farm-state income/storage/acreage stress is a real political and sectoral hit. Financial conditions have tightened into the decision date: VIX at 25.58 (+48% over the window), 10-year yields down to 2.77 from an early-November 3.24 peak, WTI down ~31% to ~$48, and a flattening 2s/10s curve—consistent with trade-war earnings and growth anxiety even though the real-side U.S. data (UMCSENT 98.3, INDPRO still rising, CPI contained) are not recessionary. The Dec 1 Meng arrest and Dec 10 detention of Kovrig/Spavor add a second front that might poison talks if Washington escalates further or if Beijing treats hostages as leverage. Action should stay near zero because (a) talks have only just opened and the May 19 joint statement already showed that purchase pledges without dates collapse within days, (b) conceding tariffs or purchases now would give away the remaining ~$267B unused tariff threat before structural terms exist, and (c) another tariff hike now would likely trigger matching Chinese retaliation and a market/farm shock while China’s own Nov IP (5.4%) and retail sales (8.1%, weakest since 2003) already give Washington leverage inside a negotiation rather than outside it.
key_factors: G20 90-day truce (Dec 1) froze the List-3 10%→25% hike but left $250B of U.S. tariffs in place
May 19 “trade war on hold” collapsed by May 29 — purchase pledges without dates are not a deal
Farm-belt pain is the main U.S. cost: China soybean purchases down 80–94%, USDA FY2019 China ag-export forecast cut $7B
U.S. real economy still resilient (sentiment, IP, CPI) while markets are stressed (VIX 25.58, 10Y 2.77, oil −31%)
Meng arrest + Kovrig/Spavor detentions raise the risk that a new escalation collapses the talks
China Nov data missed (IP 5.4%, retail 8.1%) — opponent is feeling the squeeze, which favors negotiating from the current posture
U.S. and Chinese readouts of G20 already diverge on the 90-day deadline and “lift all tariffs” language

sources_cited.excerpt: G20 Buenos Aires dinner: Trump and Xi agree to a 90-day negotiation window. Planned Jan 1, 2019 hike of List 3 from 10% to 25% is suspended (tariffs remain at 10%). Same day: Canada arrests Huawei CFO Meng Wanzhou.
China detains Canadians Michael Kovrig and Michael Spavor (widely viewed as retaliation for the Meng arrest; Beijing denies linkage).
List 3 takes effect at 10%. China imposes retaliatory tariffs (5–10%) on ~$60B of US goods. Combined US Section 301 coverage now ~$250B of Chinese imports.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
VIX latest 25.58 on 2018-12-19, change +8.25 (+47.6%) over the lookback — market stress into the decision date.
10-year Treasury yield 2.77 on 2018-12-19, down from early-November highs near 3.24 — flight-to-quality / growth-scare signal.
University of Michigan consumer sentiment 98.3 in December 2018 — still firm, not a consumer-collapse reading.
WTI crude 47.96 on 2018-12-19, down ~31% over the window.
Trump held off the Jan 1 hike on $200B; China agreed to buy a not-yet-agreed but 'very substantial' amount of ag, energy, and industrial products; existing U.S. tariffs remain on $250B.
Chinese and U.S. statements diverge: China omitted the 90-day clause and spoke of working toward lifting all tariffs; Mnuchin warned against 'soft commitments' and recalled the collapsed May truce.
China cut U.S. soybean shipments by more than 80% in September; NYT cited mid-October data showing soybean sales to China down 94% from the prior harvest.
China November industrial output 5.4% (miss vs 5.9%) and retail sales 8.1% — weakest retail pace since 2003.
Meng arrest, same day as the G20 dinner, intensified trade-war fears and risked feeding a Chinese view that the case was meant to sabotage the 90-day talks.
